bab-al-futuh.s: Bab al-Futuh is one of the monumental gates in the northern wall of Fatimid Cairo, built in the late eleventh century under the vizier Badr al-Jamali. Constructed of stone with rounded towers, it is a fine example of Fatimid military architecture.

bab-al-nasr.s: Bab al-Nasr is a fortified gate in the northern wall of Fatimid Cairo, built in the late eleventh century under the vizier Badr al-Jamali. Its square towers are decorated with carved shields and weapons.

bab-zuwayla.s: Bab Zuwayla is the southern gate of Fatimid Cairo, built in the late eleventh century under the vizier Badr al-Jamali. Its twin towers later had minarets added on top.

babur.s: Babur was a Timurid prince from Central Asia, descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, who founded the Mughal Empire. After losing his homeland in Fergana and Samarkand, he established himself in Kabul.

babylon.s: Babylon was an ancient city on the Euphrates in central Mesopotamia and one of the most famous cities of the ancient world. It was the capital of Hammurabi's Babylonian Empire and later of the Chaldean or Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II.

babylonia.s: Babylonia was the region of southern and central Mesopotamia centred on the city of Babylon. Its fertile irrigated land made it one of the wealthiest regions of the ancient Near East.

babylonian-astronomy.s: Babylonian astronomy refers to the systematic observation and mathematical prediction of celestial phenomena developed in ancient Mesopotamia, flourishing under Chaldean patronage. Its records and methods influenced Greek astronomy after Alexander's conquests.

babylonian-captivity.s: The Babylonian captivity was the period in the sixth century BCE when many inhabitants of the kingdom of Judah were deported to Babylonia by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire, following the capture of Jerusalem. The exile ended after the Persian conquest of Babylon in…

babylonian-chronicles.s: The Babylonian Chronicles are a series of cuneiform tablets recording major events in Mesopotamian history year by year, such as royal accessions, battles and festivals. They are a key source for the Neo-Babylonian period, including the campaigns of Nabopolassar and…

babylonian-invasion-of-egypt-601-bce.s: The Babylonian invasion of Egypt in 601 BCE was an attempt by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire to invade Egypt. According to the Babylonian Chronicles, the battle with the Egyptian army resulted in heavy losses on both sides, and Nebuchadnezzar withdrew.

babylonians.s: The Babylonians were the inhabitants of Babylonia in southern Mesopotamia, centred on the city of Babylon. They were long rivals of the Assyrians, and in alliance with the Medes they destroyed the Assyrian Empire at the end of the seventh century BCE.

bactria.s: Bactria was a region of Central Asia between the Hindu Kush and the Amu Darya, in present-day northern Afghanistan and neighbouring countries. It was a wealthy satrapy of the Achaemenid and Seleucid empires until its Greek governors broke away to form the Greco-Bactrian…

badajoz.s: Badajoz is a city in western Spain, near the border with Portugal. In the eleventh century it was the capital of a Muslim taifa kingdom.

badlay.s: Badlay was a sultan of Adal who led a war against the Ethiopian Empire in the fifteenth century. He was killed in 1445 at the Battle of Gomit, where his forces were defeated by Emperor Zara Yaqob.

badr-al-jamali.s: Badr al-Jamali was an Armenian commander who became vizier of the Fatimid Caliphate in 1073 after being summoned to restore order during a severe crisis. He reorganised the army and administration and rebuilt the walls and gates of Cairo, including Bab al-Futuh, Bab al-Nasr…

baggara-arabs.s: The Baggara Arabs are cattle-herding Arab groups living in the Sahel belt of present-day Sudan and Chad, including Darfur and Kordofan. They migrated into the region over several centuries.

baghdad.s: Baghdad is a city on the Tigris in Iraq, founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. It became one of the largest cities in the world and a great centre of trade and learning.

bagirmi.s: Bagirmi was a Muslim sultanate in the central Sahel, south-east of Lake Chad, founded in the sixteenth century. It was often a tributary of its more powerful neighbours, Bornu and Wadai.

bagoas.s: Bagoas was a powerful eunuch official at the Achaemenid court in the fourth century BCE. He is said to have poisoned Artaxerxes III in 338 BCE and his successor Arses, before placing Darius III on the throne.

bahadur-shah-ii.s: Bahadur Shah II, also known as Bahadur Shah Zafar, was the last Mughal emperor, whose authority by then barely extended beyond Delhi. During the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the rebels proclaimed him their leader.

bahia.s: Bahia is a state in north-eastern Brazil, with its capital at Salvador, which was the colonial capital of Brazil until 1763. It was a major destination of the Atlantic slave trade, receiving many enslaved Yoruba people as the Oyo Empire collapsed in the nineteenth century.

bahlul-lodi.s: Bahlul Lodi was an Afghan noble who founded the Lodi dynasty, the last ruling house of the Delhi Sultanate, taking power in Delhi in 1451. He restored some of the sultanate's authority in northern India, notably by conquering the Sharqi sultanate of Jaunpur.

bahmani-sultanate.s: The Bahmani Sultanate was a Muslim state in the Deccan founded in 1347 by nobles who rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughluq of Delhi. Its secession was a major loss for the Delhi Sultanate and a sign of its declining hold on the south.

bahrain.s: Bahrain is an island in the Persian Gulf. In antiquity it was probably part of Dilmun, a trading centre that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus valley in the time of the Akkadian Empire.

bahri-mamluks.s: The Bahri Mamluks were a regiment of slave soldiers formed by the Ayyubid sultan al-Salih Ayyub and stationed on an island in the Nile, from whose name ('bahr', river) they took their title. They overthrew the Ayyubids in Egypt in 1250 and defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in…

baji-rao-i.s: Baji Rao I was the Peshwa, or chief minister, of the Maratha state from 1720 to 1740. A brilliant cavalry commander, he led rapid campaigns that extended Maratha power deep into northern India, raiding as far as Delhi.

bakhtiari.s: The Bakhtiari are a tribal people of the Zagros Mountains in south-western Iran, traditionally pastoral nomads. They were a significant military force in Iranian politics.

baku.s: Baku is a city on the western shore of the Caspian Sea and the capital of present-day Azerbaijan. It was annexed by the Russian Empire in the early nineteenth century.

balaji-vishwanath.s: Balaji Vishwanath was the first of the hereditary Peshwas of the Maratha state, serving from 1713 to 1720. He helped Shahu secure the Maratha throne and negotiated recognition from the Mughals of Maratha rights to collect revenue in the Deccan.

balban.s: Balban was a sultan of the Delhi Sultanate who assumed the throne in 1266, after serving as a powerful minister. He strengthened royal authority by breaking the power of the Turkic nobles, maintaining a strict court ceremonial and an extensive spy network.

bale.s: Bale is a region in south-eastern Ethiopia. In the fourteenth century it was one of the territories incorporated into the Christian Ethiopian state through the expansion of Amda Seyon.

balearic-islands.s: The Balearic Islands are an archipelago in the western Mediterranean, including Majorca, Minorca and Ibiza. Ibiza was a Phoenician and later Carthaginian colony, and the islands were part of the Punic Empire's network.

bali.s: Bali is an island in the Indonesian archipelago east of Java. It was conquered by the Majapahit Empire in the fourteenth century.

balkan-wars.s: The Balkan Wars were two wars fought in 1912–1913 in south-eastern Europe. In the first, Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro defeated the Ottoman Empire and took almost all its remaining European territory.

balkans.s: The Balkans are the peninsula of south-eastern Europe between the Adriatic, Aegean and Black seas. The region was a core part of the Byzantine Empire and later of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled it for centuries.

balopwe.s: Balopwe refers to the sacred quality of kingship in the Luba Empire, believed to be transmitted through the royal bloodline. Those possessing it could claim the right to rule.

baltic-fleet.s: The Baltic Fleet is the branch of the Russian navy based on the Baltic Sea. During the Russo-Japanese War much of it was sent around the world as the Second Pacific Squadron.

baltic-sea.s: The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic in northern Europe, bordered by Scandinavia, Germany, Poland, the Baltic states and Russia. Control of its trade and coasts was the central aim of the Swedish Empire in the seventeenth century, and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth…

bamangwato.s: The BaMangwato are a Tswana people of present-day Botswana. In the eighteenth century they lived to the south-west of the Rozvi Empire's territory.

bambudye.s: The Bambudye was a secret society in the Luba Empire that guarded royal history, rituals and political knowledge. Its members used memory devices called lukasa to preserve and interpret the kingdom's history.

bambuk.s: Bambuk is a gold-bearing region in West Africa, between the Senegal and Falémé rivers in present-day Senegal and Mali. Its gold fields were a major source of the gold traded across the Sahara.

banda-islands.s: The Banda Islands are a small group of islands in eastern Indonesia that were the world's only source of nutmeg and mace in the early modern period. The Dutch East India Company conquered them in 1621, killing or expelling most of the inhabitants.

bandar-abbas.s: Bandar Abbas is a port on the Persian Gulf coast of southern Iran, named after Shah Abbas I, who developed it after capturing Hormuz from the Portuguese in 1622. It became Iran's main port for trade with European companies.

bandar-rig.s: Bandar Rig is a small port on the Persian Gulf coast of Iran. It is mentioned in the Zand Empire's profile in connection with the Gulf coast where European companies, including the British East India Company and the Dutch VOC, established commercial presences.

band-e-kaisar.s: The Band-e Kaisar was a combined bridge and dam on the Karun River at Shushtar in south-western Iran, built under the Sasanian Empire in the third century. Tradition holds that it was built with the labour of Roman prisoners captured by Shapur I.

bank-of-brazil.s: The Bank of Brazil was founded in 1808 by the Portuguese prince regent João after the royal court moved to Rio de Janeiro. It was reorganised several times during the nineteenth century.

bank-of-england.s: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to lend money to the English government, primarily to finance war against France. It managed government debt and became the central bank of the United Kingdom.

bantu-peoples.s: The Bantu peoples are the large family of peoples speaking Bantu languages, spread across Central, East and Southern Africa. Their expansion over many centuries carried agriculture and iron-working across much of the continent.

banu-umayya.s: The Banu Umayya was a powerful clan of the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. The third caliph, Uthman, belonged to it, and his favouring of kinsmen in appointments caused discontent that contributed to the Rashidun Caliphate's crisis.

baol.s: Baol was a Wolof kingdom in present-day Senegal that was a vassal state within the Jolof Empire. After Jolof's defeat at the Battle of Danki around 1549, Baol, along with Cayor and others, became independent.

barakzai-dynasty.s: The Barakzai dynasty was the ruling family of Afghanistan from the nineteenth century, whose most notable early figure was Dost Mohammad Khan. It replaced the Durrani Sadozai line.

barattarna.s: Barattarna was an early king of Mitanni around c. 1500 BCE.

barcid-family.s: The Barcid family was a leading Carthaginian family of the third century BCE, including Hamilcar Barca and his sons Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Mago. After the First Punic War they built a power base in Spain, rich in silver mines.

barentu-oromo.s: The Barentu Oromo are one of the two main branches of the Oromo people of Ethiopia. During the great Oromo migrations of the sixteenth century they moved into the lowlands and plateau around Harar.

bariba.s: The Bariba are a people of Borgu, in present-day northern Benin and western Nigeria. In the early centuries of the Oyo Empire they exerted military pressure on Oyo from the north-west.

barlas.s: The Barlas were a Mongol tribe that settled in Transoxiana and became largely Turkic in language and Muslim in faith. They held lands around Kesh in the Chagatai realm.

barmakids.s: The Barmakids were a family of Iranian origin, from Balkh, who served as viziers and administrators to the early Abbasid caliphs. They held great influence under Harun al-Rashid, patronising scholarship and organising government.

bartolome-de-las-casas.s: Bartolomé de las Casas was a Spanish Dominican friar of the sixteenth century who became a leading critic of the treatment of indigenous peoples in the Americas. His writings denounced abuses by colonists and the encomienda system.

bartolomeu-dias.s: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese navigator who in 1488 became the first European known to sail around the southern tip of Africa, the Cape of Good Hope. His voyage proved that the Atlantic connected with the Indian Ocean.

basf.s: BASF is a German chemical company founded in 1865. It became one of the world's leading producers of synthetic dyes and later developed the industrial synthesis of ammonia.

basil-ii.s: Basil II was Byzantine emperor from 976 to 1025, one of the most successful rulers of the empire. After a long war he conquered the Bulgarian state, earning the epithet 'the Bulgar-Slayer'.

basileus.s: Basileus is a Greek word for king. Alexander's successors, including Seleucus I, adopted the title to assert their sovereignty over the territories they held.

basilike-chora.s: The basilike chora, meaning 'royal land', was land held directly by the king in the Hellenistic kingdoms. In the Seleucid Empire it was worked by dependent peasants who paid rents or taxes to the crown, while other land belonged to cities or temples.

basmyls.s: The Basmyls were a Turkic tribe of Central Asia. In 744 CE they joined the Uyghurs and Karluks in seizing Ötüken and killing the last Göktürk khagan.

basorun.s: The Basorun was the head of the Oyo Mesi, the council of seven hereditary chiefs in the Oyo Empire. The Basorun led the council that could check the Alaafin and, according to custom, call on him to die.

basorun-gaa.s: Basorun Gaa was the head of the Oyo Mesi council who dominated the Oyo Empire from around the 1740s until he was executed c. 1774.

basorun-gaa-crisis.s: The Basorun Gaa crisis was the period of c. 1745–1774 when the Basorun Gaa, head of the Oyo Mesi council, dominated the Oyo Empire and several Alaafins were compelled to die.

basques.s: The Basques are a people of the western Pyrenees, in northern Spain and south-western France, with a distinct language unrelated to other European languages. In 778 Basque forces ambushed the rearguard of Charlemagne's army at Roncevaux Pass.

basra.s: Basra is a port city in southern Iraq, founded around 636 as a garrison town of the Rashidun Caliphate. It became a major commercial and intellectual centre of the early Islamic world.

batavia.s: Batavia, now Jakarta, was a city on the north-west coast of Java founded by the Dutch East India Company in 1619. It became the headquarters of the company's operations in Asia and the capital of the Dutch East Indies.

batavian-republic.s: The Batavian Republic was the state that replaced the Dutch Republic in 1795 after French revolutionary forces occupied the Netherlands. It was a French client state, and during this period the Dutch East India Company was nationalised and dissolved.

battering-ram.s: A battering ram is a siege weapon consisting of a heavy beam used to break down gates and walls. The Assyrian army developed wheeled, armoured siege engines with rams, shown on palace reliefs.

battle-of-abeche.s: The Battle of Abéché was the French capture of Abéché, capital of the Wadai Empire, in 1909. French colonial forces defeated the sultan's army and occupied the city.

battle-of-actium.s: The Battle of Actium was a naval battle fought in 31 BCE off western Greece between Octavian and the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII. Octavian's fleet under Agrippa won decisively.

battle-of-adrianople.s: The Battle of Adrianople was fought in 378 CE in Thrace between the Roman army under the eastern emperor Valens and Gothic forces. The Romans were heavily defeated and Valens was killed.

battle-of-adwa.s: The Battle of Adwa was fought in 1896 in northern Ethiopia between the forces of Emperor Menelik II and an invading Italian army. The Ethiopians won a decisive victory, forcing Italy to recognise Ethiopian independence.

battle-of-ain-jalut.s: The Battle of Ain Jalut was fought in 1260 in Palestine between the Mamluk Sultanate and a Mongol army of the Ilkhanate. The Mamluks under Qutuz and Baybars won, halting the Mongol advance into Egypt.

battle-of-alarcos.s: The Battle of Alarcos was fought in 1195 in central Spain between the Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur and King Alfonso VIII of Castile. The Almohads won a major victory.

battle-of-al-buhayra.s: The Battle of al-Buhayra was fought in 1130 near Marrakesh between the early Almohad movement and the Almoravids. The Almohads suffered a catastrophic defeat.

battle-of-alcacer-quibir.s: The Battle of Alcácer Quibir, also called the Battle of the Three Kings, was fought in northern Morocco in 1578. A Portuguese army under King Sebastian was destroyed by Moroccan forces, and Sebastian was killed along with much of the nobility.

battle-of-alkalawa.s: The Battle of Alkalawa was the capture in 1808 of Alkalawa, the capital of the Hausa kingdom of Gobir, by the forces of Usman dan Fodio's jihad. The Gobir ruler was killed.

battle-of-al-qadisiyyah.s: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah was fought in 636 or 637 CE in southern Iraq between the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate and the Sasanian Empire. The Arab forces won a decisive victory over the Sasanian army.

battle-of-amba-sel.s: The Battle of Amba Sel was fought in 1531 in the Ethiopian highlands between the forces of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi of Adal and the army of the Ethiopian emperor Lebna Dengel. Adal won, continuing its advance into the Christian highlands.

battle-of-ankara.s: The Battle of Ankara was fought in 1402 in central Anatolia between Timur and the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I. Timur won a crushing victory and captured Bayezid, who died in captivity.

battle-of-ansata.s: The Battle of Ansata was fought in 1270 in Ethiopia, when Yekuno Amlak defeated the last ruler of the Zagwe dynasty. Yekuno Amlak then took the throne and founded the Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

battle-of-arsuf.s: The Battle of Arsuf was fought in 1191 on the coast of Palestine during the Third Crusade, between the Crusader army of Richard I of England and Saladin's forces. The Crusaders won, allowing them to secure Jaffa.

battle-of-assaye.s: The Battle of Assaye was fought in 1803 in western India during the Second Anglo-Maratha War. A British force under Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, defeated a much larger army of the Maratha chiefs Scindia and the Bhonsle of Nagpur.

battle-of-baideng.s: The Battle of Baideng took place in 200 BCE near present-day Datong in northern China. The Xiongnu ruler Modu Chanyu surrounded the Han emperor Gaozu and his army, and the emperor escaped only after negotiations.

battle-of-bapheus.s: The Battle of Bapheus was fought in 1301 near Nicomedia in north-western Anatolia between the forces of Osman I and a Byzantine army. Osman's victory brought him prestige and attracted followers to his principality.

battle-of-birinjiya.s: The Battle of Birinjiya was fought in 1916 near El Fasher between a British-led Anglo-Egyptian force and the army of Sultan Ali Dinar of Darfur. Darfur's forces, lacking artillery and modern weapons, were defeated.

battle-of-breitenfeld-1631.s: The Battle of Breitenfeld was fought in 1631 near Leipzig during the Thirty Years' War. The Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus, with Saxon allies, decisively defeated the Catholic imperial army under Tilly.

battle-of-burmi.s: The Battle of Burmi was fought in 1903 in north-eastern Nigeria between British colonial forces and followers of the deposed caliph Attahiru I, who had fled after the fall of Sokoto. Attahiru was killed in the battle.

battle-of-cannae.s: The Battle of Cannae was fought in 216 BCE in south-eastern Italy during the Second Punic War. Hannibal's Carthaginian army encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army.

battle-of-carchemish.s: The Battle of Carchemish was fought in 605 BCE at Carchemish on the Euphrates. The Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptian army and the remnants of Assyrian forces.

battle-of-carrhae.s: The Battle of Carrhae was fought in 53 BCE near Carrhae (Harran) in upper Mesopotamia. A Parthian army of horse archers and heavy cavalry under the general Surena destroyed a Roman army led by Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was killed.

battle-of-chaldiran.s: The Battle of Chaldiran was fought in 1514 in north-western Iran between the Ottoman sultan Selim I and the Safavid shah Ismail I. The Ottomans, using artillery and firearms, won a decisive victory over the Safavid cavalry.

battle-of-corupedium.s: The Battle of Corupedium was fought in 281 BCE in western Anatolia between Seleucus I and Lysimachus, two of Alexander's successors. Lysimachus was killed, and Seleucus gained control of Asia Minor.

battle-of-dandanaqan.s: The Battle of Dandanaqan was fought in 1040 near Merv between the Seljuk Turks and the Ghaznavid army of Sultan Mas'ud. The Seljuks won a decisive victory.

battle-of-danki.s: The Battle of Danki was fought around c. 1549 in present-day Senegal between the forces of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall of Cayor and the army of the Jolof Empire.

battle-of-der.s: The Battle of Der was fought in 721 BCE near the city of Der in eastern Mesopotamia between the Assyrian king Sargon II and the Elamite king, allied with the Babylonian ruler Merodach-baladan. Assyrian and Babylonian sources give conflicting claims of victory, but the Elamites…

battle-of-dien-bien-phu.s: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu was fought in 1954 in northern Vietnam between the French army and the Viet Minh under General Vo Nguyen Giap. The Viet Minh besieged and captured the French base.

battle-of-dingjiazhou.s: The Battle of Dingjiazhou was fought in 1275 on the Yangtze River between the Mongol forces of Kublai Khan and the Southern Song army commanded by Jia Sidao. The Song army collapsed.

battle-of-diu-1509.s: The Battle of Diu was a naval battle fought in 1509 off Diu on the west coast of India. A Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida defeated a combined fleet of the Mamluk Sultanate, the Sultanate of Gujarat and the Zamorin of Calicut.

battle-of-edessa.s: The Battle of Edessa was fought in 260 CE in upper Mesopotamia between the Roman emperor Valerian and the Sasanian king Shapur I. The Roman army was defeated and Valerian was captured, the first Roman emperor to be taken prisoner.

battle-of-fatagar.s: The Battle of Fatagar was fought in 1559 between the forces of Emir Nur ibn Mujahid of Adal and the Ethiopian emperor Gelawdewos, who was killed. Although Adal won, it could not restore its earlier dominance.

battle-of-feyiase.s: The Battle of Feyiase was fought in 1701 between the Asante and the Denkyira, the dominant Akan power of the region to which the Asante had paid tribute. The Asante, under Osei Tutu, won a decisive victory.

battle-of-fontenoy.s: The Battle of Fontenoy was fought in 841 CE in Burgundy between the Carolingian emperor Lothair I and his brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald. Lothair was defeated in a very bloody battle.

battle-of-gaugamela.s: The Battle of Gaugamela was fought in 331 BCE in northern Mesopotamia between Alexander the Great and the Achaemenid king Darius III. Despite being outnumbered, Alexander won a decisive victory and Darius fled.

battle-of-gaza-312-bce.s: The Battle of Gaza was fought in 312 BCE between Demetrius, son of Antigonus I, and the forces of Ptolemy I and Seleucus. Ptolemy and Seleucus won.

battle-of-gomit.s: The Battle of Gomit was fought in 1445 in Ethiopia between the Ethiopian emperor Zara Yaqob and Sultan Badlay of Adal. Badlay was killed and his army defeated.

battle-of-gulnabad.s: The Battle of Gulnabad was fought in 1722 near Isfahan between an Afghan army led by Mahmud Hotaki and the Safavid army. The much larger Safavid force was defeated.

battle-of-hattin.s: The Battle of Hattin was fought in 1187 near Tiberias in Galilee between Saladin and the army of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin destroyed the Crusader army and captured its king.

battle-of-hazalo.s: The Battle of Hazalo was a defeat suffered by the army of Emir Nur ibn Mujahid of Adal in the period after Imam Ahmad's death. Harar's walls could protect the city but not the surrounding countryside.

battle-of-holowczyn.s: The Battle of Holowczyn was fought in 1708 in present-day Belarus during the Great Northern War. Charles XII of Sweden defeated a Russian army in what was one of his last major victories.

battle-of-hormozdgan.s: The Battle of Hormozdgan was fought in 224 CE between Ardashir I and the Parthian king Artabanus IV. Artabanus was killed, and Ardashir was soon crowned king of kings.

battle-of-ipsus.s: The Battle of Ipsus was fought in 301 BCE in Phrygia between Antigonus I and his son Demetrius on one side and a coalition of Seleucus I, Lysimachus and Cassander on the other. Seleucus's war elephants played an important role, and Antigonus was killed.

battle-of-issus.s: The Battle of Issus was fought in 333 BCE near the Gulf of Issus in south-eastern Anatolia between Alexander the Great and Darius III. Alexander won, and Darius fled, leaving his family to be captured.

battle-of-kadesh.s: The Battle of Kadesh was fought in 1274 BCE near Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria between the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II. It is one of the best-documented chariot battles of antiquity and ended without a decisive result, despite Egyptian…

battle-of-kansala.s: The Battle of Kansala was the siege of Kansala, capital of the Kaabu Empire, in 1867 by Fula forces from Futa Jallon and allies. Facing defeat, the Kaabu ruler is said to have blown up the city's gunpowder store, killing defenders and attackers alike.

battle-of-karbala.s: The Battle of Karbala was fought in 680 CE in Iraq between the forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. Husayn and most of his small band were killed.

battle-of-karnal.s: The Battle of Karnal was fought in 1739 north of Delhi between Nader Shah of Iran and the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah. Nader's army won a decisive victory, and he went on to occupy and plunder Delhi, taking the Peacock Throne.

battle-of-katamansu.s: The Battle of Katamansu was fought in 1826 near Accra between the Ashanti army and a coalition of coastal peoples supported by the British. The Ashanti were defeated, partly by the use of Congreve rockets.

battle-of-khanwa.s: The Battle of Khanwa was fought in 1527 in northern India between Babur and a Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar. Babur's forces, using field artillery and firearms, won a decisive victory.

battle-of-kircholm.s: The Battle of Kircholm was fought in 1605 near Riga between the army of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and a larger Swedish army. Commonwealth forces under Jan Karol Chodkiewicz, led by the winged hussar cavalry, won a crushing victory.

battle-of-kirina.s: The Battle of Kirina was fought around c. 1235 in West Africa between Sundiata Keita and Sumanguru Kante, ruler of the Sosso kingdom.

battle-of-klushino.s: The Battle of Klushino was fought in 1610 during the Polish-Muscovite War. A small Polish-Lithuanian army under Stanisław Żółkiewski, led by hussar cavalry, defeated a larger Russian and Swedish mercenary force.

battle-of-kose-dag.s: The Battle of Köse Dağ was fought in 1243 in north-eastern Anatolia between the Mongols and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. The Mongols won decisively, reducing the Seljuks of Rum to vassals.

battle-of-lagos-1759.s: The Battle of Lagos was a naval battle fought in 1759 off the coast of Portugal during the Seven Years' War. A British fleet under Admiral Edward Boscawen defeated a French squadron trying to leave the Mediterranean.

battle-of-lake-trasimene.s: The Battle of Lake Trasimene was fought in 217 BCE in central Italy during the Second Punic War. Hannibal ambushed a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius along the lake shore, destroying it and killing Flaminius.

battle-of-las-navas-de-tolosa.n: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
battle-of-las-navas-de-tolosa.s: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa was fought in 1212 in southern Spain between the Almohad Caliphate and a coalition of the Christian kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, Navarre and Portugal, assembled under a papal crusade declaration. The Almohad army was shattered and the caliph…

battle-of-lechfeld.s: The Battle of Lechfeld was fought in 955 CE near Augsburg, where Otto I of Saxony decisively defeated the invading Magyars. The victory ended the Magyar raids into the German lands and greatly enhanced Otto's prestige.

battle-of-legnano.s: The Battle of Legnano was fought in 1176 in northern Italy, where the forces of the Lombard League defeated the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. The defeat showed the limits of imperial military power, which depended on princely contingents that could not be…

battle-of-lutzen-1632.s: The Battle of Lützen was fought in 1632 in Saxony during the Thirty Years' War between the Swedish army and imperial forces under Wallenstein. The Swedes held the field, but King Gustavus Adolphus was killed during the fighting.

battle-of-magnesia.s: The Battle of Magnesia was fought in 190 BCE in western Anatolia between the Roman Republic, supported by Pergamene allies, and the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III. A Roman army of about 30,000 comprehensively destroyed a far larger Seleucid force.

battle-of-manawashi.s: The Battle of Manawashi was fought in 1874 in Darfur, where the forces of the Sudanese slave-trading warlord al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur, operating with tacit Egyptian backing, defeated the army of Sultan Ibrahim. The Darfuri cavalry was decisively beaten and the sultan was killed.

battle-of-manzikert.s: The Battle of Manzikert was fought in 1071 in eastern Anatolia between the Byzantine Empire under Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes and the Seljuk Turks under Sultan Alp Arslan. The Byzantine army was defeated and the emperor captured.

battle-of-marathon.s: The Battle of Marathon was fought in 490 BCE on the plain of Marathon in Attica, where an Athenian army, aided by Plataea, defeated a Persian expeditionary force sent by Darius I. It ended the first Persian invasion of Greece.

battle-of-marj-dabiq.s: The Battle of Marj Dabiq was fought in 1516 near Aleppo in northern Syria between the Ottoman Empire under Selim I and the Mamluk Sultanate. The Mamluk army was decisively defeated and Sultan al-Ghawri was killed.

battle-of-maungwe.s: The Battle of Maungwe was fought in 1684 in the Zimbabwe plateau, where Changamire Dombo defeated a combined punitive force of Mutapa troops and their Portuguese allies. The victory simultaneously asserted independence from an African overlord and repelled European colonial…

battle-of-mbwila.s: The Battle of Mbwila was fought in 1665 between the Kingdom of Kongo and Portuguese forces from Angola with their African allies. Kongo was defeated and its king, António I, was killed.

battle-of-megiddo.s: The Battle of Megiddo, dated by the site to 1457 BCE, was fought in northern Canaan between Egypt under Thutmose III and a coalition of Canaanite rulers led by the king of Kadesh. The Egyptian victory, followed by a siege of Megiddo, is one of the earliest battles recorded in…

battle-of-midway.s: The Battle of Midway was a naval and air battle fought in June 1942 near Midway Atoll in the central Pacific during the Second World War. United States forces sank four Japanese fleet carriers, inflicting losses the Empire of Japan could not replace.

battle-of-ming-sha.s: The Battle of Ming Sha was an engagement of the Second Göktürk Khaganate in which a Tang army reported at 80,000 was defeated by a significantly smaller Göktürk force. It belongs to the era of Qapaghan Qaghan, whose campaigns forced Tang tribute payments.

battle-of-mohacs.s: The Battle of Mohács was fought in 1526 in southern Hungary between the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent and the Kingdom of Hungary. The Hungarian army was annihilated and King Louis II died during the retreat.

battle-of-narva-1700.s: The Battle of Narva was fought in 1700 at the start of the Great Northern War, when about 8,000 Swedish troops under Charles XII routed a much larger Russian army besieging Narva. It was one of the finest tactical victories of the Swedish Empire.

battle-of-navarino.s: The Battle of Navarino was a naval battle fought in 1827 in the bay of Navarino in the Peloponnese during the Greek War of Independence. A combined British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet.

battle-of-nihawand.s: The Battle of Nihawand was fought in 642 CE in western Iran between the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate and the forces of the Sasanian Empire. Called the "Victory of Victories" in Islamic tradition, it effectively destroyed the remaining organised Sasanian military capacity.

battle-of-nineveh-627.s: The Battle of Nineveh was fought in 627 CE near the ruins of ancient Nineveh in northern Mesopotamia, where the Byzantine emperor Heraclius defeated a Sasanian army. It was the climax of the Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602–628.

battle-of-nowshera.s: The Battle of Nowshera was fought in 1823 near the Kabul River in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent between the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh and Afghan forces. The Sikh victory demonstrated the effectiveness of the Europeanised infantry-artillery combination working…

battle-of-nsamankow.s: The Battle of Nsamankow was fought on 22 January 1824 in the Gold Coast, where an army of the Ashanti Empire annihilated a British expeditionary force under Governor Sir Charles MacCarthy, who was killed. It was one of the most significant defeats suffered by British forces in…

battle-of-opis.s: The Battle of Opis was fought in 539 BCE near the Tigris in Mesopotamia, where the Persian forces of Cyrus the Great defeated the Babylonian army. Babylon itself then fell without meaningful resistance.

battle-of-ourique.s: The Battle of Ourique was fought in 1139 in the south of present-day Portugal, where Afonso Henriques defeated Muslim forces. The victory became the traditional founding moment of the independent Kingdom of Portugal.

battle-of-panium.s: The Battle of Panium was fought around 200 BCE near the sources of the Jordan River during the Fifth Syrian War, between the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III and the Ptolemaic army under Scopas. Seleucid cavalry encircled and destroyed the Ptolemaic force.

battle-of-pavia.s: The Battle of Pavia was fought in 1525 in northern Italy during the Italian Wars, between the forces of Charles V and the French army of Francis I. The imperial and Spanish army won a decisive victory and captured the French king.

battle-of-pelusium.s: The Battle of Pelusium was fought in 525 BCE at the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, where the Persian king Cambyses II defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III. The victory completed the conquests begun by Cyrus the Great.

battle-of-plataea.s: The Battle of Plataea was fought in 479 BCE in Boeotia, where an allied Greek army led by Sparta defeated the Persian land forces under Mardonius. It ended the second Persian invasion of Greece.

battle-of-poltava.s: The Battle of Poltava was fought in 1709 in present-day Ukraine during the Great Northern War, where the army of Peter I of Russia decisively defeated Charles XII of Sweden. The Swedish army was destroyed and its remnants capitulated soon afterwards.

battle-of-qatwan.s: The Battle of Qatwan was fought in 1141 near Samarkand, where the Qara Khitai, a Buddhist Sinicised steppe power, defeated the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar. The defeat destroyed Seljuk authority in Central Asia.

battle-of-quiberon-bay.s: The Battle of Quiberon Bay was a naval battle fought in November 1759 off the coast of Brittany during the Seven Years' War. The British fleet under Admiral Hawke defeated the French fleet, ending French plans to invade Britain.

battle-of-raphia.s: The Battle of Raphia was fought in 217 BCE near Gaza during the Fourth Syrian War, between Ptolemy IV of Egypt and the Seleucid king Antiochus III. The Ptolemaic army won, with native Egyptian troops playing a significant role.

battle-of-rocroi.s: The Battle of Rocroi was fought in 1643 in northern France during the Thirty Years' War, where a French army under the Duke of Enghien defeated the Spanish Army of Flanders. The Spanish tercios, long considered the finest infantry in Europe, suffered heavy losses.

battle-of-roncevaux-pass.s: The Battle of Roncevaux Pass was fought in 778 in the Pyrenees, where Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed and destroyed by Basques during the withdrawal from a failed Spanish campaign. The event demonstrated the geographic limits of the Carolingian military machine.

battle-of-sagrajas.s: The Battle of Sagrajas, called Zallaca in Arabic, was fought on 23 October 1086 near Badajoz, where Yusuf ibn Tashfin's Almoravid army shattered the forces of Alfonso VI of Castile. The victory showed the effectiveness of Almoravid Saharan tactics, including drums and camels.

battle-of-sekigahara.s: The Battle of Sekigahara was fought in 1600 in central Japan between the forces of Tokugawa Ieyasu and a coalition of rival daimyo loyal to the Toyotomi house. Ieyasu's victory made him the dominant power in Japan.

battle-of-sharur.s: The Battle of Sharur was fought in 1501 in the southern Caucasus, where Ismail, head of the Safaviyya order, led the Qizilbash to victory over the Aq Qoyunlu confederation. Ismail then seized Tabriz and declared himself Shah of Iran.

battle-of-shimbra-kure.s: The Battle of Shimbra Kure was fought in March 1529 in the Ethiopian highlands, where the forces of the Adal Sultanate under Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi routed a much larger army of the Ethiopian Empire. Ahmad's victory rested on Ottoman-supplied firearms and disciplined use of…

battle-of-siffin.s: The Battle of Siffin was fought in 657 CE on the Euphrates in Syria between the caliph Ali and Mu'awiya, the governor of Syria, during the First Fitna. The fighting ended inconclusively in arbitration, which divided Ali's supporters and led to the secession of the Kharijites.

battle-of-sobraon.s: The Battle of Sobraon was fought in 1846 on the Sutlej River and was the decisive engagement of the First Anglo-Sikh War. The British East India Company's forces defeated the Sikh army, weakened by divisions within its own court.

battle-of-talas.s: The Battle of Talas was fought in 751 near the Talas River in Central Asia, where a Tang army was defeated by an Abbasid-allied force. It is often cited as a marker of the limit of Tang Dynasty expansion westward.

battle-of-tarain-1215.s: The Battle of Tarain of 1215 was fought in northern India, where Sultan Iltutmish defeated rival claimants to power, notably Taj al-Din Yildiz. It took place on the same field as the better-known battles of 1191 and 1192.

battle-of-the-aegates.s: The Battle of the Aegates was a naval battle fought in 241 BCE off the western coast of Sicily, in which the Roman fleet defeated the Carthaginian navy. It ended the First Punic War.

battle-of-the-camel.s: The Battle of the Camel was fought in 656 CE near Basra between the caliph Ali and forces led by Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr, who demanded vengeance for the murdered caliph Uthman. It takes its name from the camel on which Aisha rode during the fighting.

battle-of-the-granicus.s: The Battle of the Granicus was fought in 334 BCE at the Granicus River in northwestern Anatolia, the first major victory of Alexander the Great over the Persian satraps. It opened Asia Minor to the Macedonian Empire.

battle-of-the-great-zab.s: The Battle of the Great Zab was fought in January 750 on the Great Zab River in northern Iraq, where the forces of the Abbasid Revolution defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II. Marwan fled to Egypt, where he was killed.

battle-of-the-java-sea.s: The Battle of the Java Sea was a naval battle fought on 27 February 1942 during the Second World War, in which a Japanese fleet defeated an Allied squadron of Dutch, British, Australian and American ships. The defeat opened Java to Japanese invasion.

battle-of-the-somme.s: The Battle of the Somme was fought from July to November 1916 in northern France during the First World War, between British and French forces and the army of the German Empire. It was one of the bloodiest battles in history, with enormous losses on both sides and little…

battle-of-the-teutoburg-forest.s: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest was fought in 9 CE in Germania, where Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus. It was one of the worst defeats in Roman military history.

battle-of-the-trebia.s: The Battle of the Trebia was fought in 218 BCE in northern Italy, the first major victory of Hannibal over the Romans after his crossing of the Alps during the Second Punic War. A Roman army was lured across the river and caught in an ambush.

battle-of-the-yarmuk.s: The Battle of the Yarmuk was fought in August 636 CE near the Yarmuk River in the Levant, where the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate decisively defeated the Byzantine army. The defeat ended Byzantine rule over Syria.

battle-of-thermopylae.s: The Battle of Thermopylae was fought in 480 BCE at a narrow coastal pass in central Greece, where a small Greek force led by King Leonidas of Sparta held off the army of Xerxes I for several days. The Persians eventually outflanked the defenders and destroyed them.

battle-of-thymbra.s: The Battle of Thymbra was fought in 546 BCE in western Anatolia, where Cyrus the Great defeated Croesus of Lydia. Cyrus then captured Sardis and brought the Ionian Greek cities of the Aegean coast under Persian rule.

battle-of-tondibi.s: The Battle of Tondibi was fought on 12 March 1591 near the Niger River, where a Moroccan expeditionary force under Judar Pasha, armed with arquebuses and light cannon, routed the much larger army of the Songhai Empire under Askia Ishaq II. The battle showed the overwhelming…

battle-of-tours.s: The Battle of Tours, also called the Battle of Poitiers, was fought in 732 CE in western France, where Frankish forces under Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. It halted the northward advance of the Umayyad Caliphate from Iberia.

battle-of-trafalgar.s: The Battle of Trafalgar was a naval battle fought in 1805 off Cape Trafalgar in southwestern Spain, in which the British fleet under Admiral Nelson defeated the combined fleets of France and Spain. Nelson was killed during the battle.

battle-of-tsushima.s: The Battle of Tsushima was a naval battle fought in May 1905 in the strait between Korea and Japan, the decisive engagement of the Russo-Japanese War. The Japanese fleet under Admiral Togo destroyed the Russian fleet that had sailed from the Baltic.

battle-of-verdun.s: The Battle of Verdun was fought in 1916 in northeastern France during the First World War, between the armies of the German Empire and France. It was one of the longest and costliest battles of the war, and ended without a decisive result.

battle-of-vienna-1683.s: The Battle of Vienna was fought in 1683, when a relief army led by King John III Sobieski of Poland broke the Ottoman siege of the Habsburg capital. The failed siege ended the westward advance of the Ottoman Empire into Central Europe.

battle-of-wadi-al-khaznadar.s: The Battle of Wadi al-Khaznadar was fought in 1299 near Homs in Syria, where the Ilkhanate under Ghazan Khan defeated the army of the Mamluk Sultanate. It was the only major Mongol victory in the long conflict between the two powers.

battle-of-waterloo.s: The Battle of Waterloo was fought in June 1815 in present-day Belgium, where an Anglo-allied army under the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Blücher defeated Napoleon. It ended the Napoleonic Wars.

battle-of-wayna-daga.s: The Battle of Wayna Daga was fought on 21 February 1543 in the Ethiopian highlands, where Emperor Galawdewos of the Ethiopian Empire, aided by Portuguese musketeers, defeated and killed Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known as Ahmad Gran. The Portuguese contingent had arrived…

battle-of-webi-river.s: The Battle of Webi River was a late sixteenth-century engagement in the Horn of Africa in which the Adalite leader Muhammad ibn Nasir was killed. Together with Emperor Sarsa Dengel's defeat and execution of Sultan Muhammad V in 1577, it permanently ended the Adal Sultanate as…

battle-of-yamama.s: The Battle of Yamama was fought in central Arabia during the Ridda Wars of 632–633 CE, between the forces of the caliph Abu Bakr and the followers of the rival prophetic claimant Musaylima. The caliphal army, led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, won a hard-fought victory and Musaylima…

battle-of-yamen.s: The Battle of Yamen was a naval battle fought in March 1279 off the southern coast of China, in which the Yuan fleet destroyed the last loyalist fleet of the Song Dynasty. The young last Song emperor was drowned by his minister to prevent his capture.

bayan-wujub-al-hijra.s: Bayan Wujub al-Hijra (Exposition on the Obligation of Migration) is a political and religious treatise by Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate. It sets out the duty of Muslims to leave lands ruled unjustly and the obligations of an Islamic government.

baybars.s: Baybars, or Baybars I, was a Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria who reigned from 1260 to 1277. As a general he shared in the victory over the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, before seizing the throne.

bayer.s: Bayer is a German chemical and pharmaceutical company founded in the nineteenth century. Along with BASF and Hoechst, it led the chemical industry of the German Empire, which by 1913 dominated the global market for synthetic dyes.

bayezid-i.s: Bayezid I was an Ottoman sultan of the late fourteenth century, known for rapid conquests in the Balkans and Anatolia. He was defeated and captured by Timur at the Battle of Ankara in 1402.

bazaar.s: A bazaar is a market or commercial quarter, typically of covered streets, shops and workshops, found in cities across the Islamic world and South Asia. In the Safavid Empire the bazaars of Isfahan linked Indian Ocean imports with European demand, while those of Lahore…

bead.s: Beads are small decorative objects of glass, stone, shell or metal, pierced for threading, which served widely as trade goods and stores of value. Sub-Saharan beads found at Garamantian sites illustrate the reach of the Garamantian Empire's trans-Saharan exchange.

beas.s: The Beas is a river of northern India, one of the five rivers that give the Punjab its name, alongside the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej. It rises in the Himalayas and joins the Sutlej.

beglarbegi.s: Beglarbegi, meaning "bey of beys", was the title of a provincial military governor in the Safavid Empire. Safavid provincial government was divided between these military governors and fiscal administrators called vazirs.

behistun-inscription.s: The Behistun Inscription is a monumental rock relief and text carved on a cliff in western Iran on the orders of the Achaemenid king Darius I, recording his accession and victories. It is written in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

beijing.s: Beijing is a city in northern China that has served as the capital of several imperial dynasties. As Dadu (Khanbaliq) it was the capital of the Yuan Dynasty, and the Ming Empire moved its capital there in the early fifteenth century, building the Forbidden City.

beirut.s: Beirut is a port city on the eastern Mediterranean coast, now the capital of Lebanon. In the medieval period it was one of the coastal ports, along with Acre and Tyre, that connected overland routes from the Persian Gulf and Central Asia to Mediterranean trade.

bek.s: The bek, or khagan-bek, was the executive ruler in the dual kingship system of the Khazar Khaganate. While the khagan served as a sacred figurehead embodying divine legitimacy, the bek exercised practical political and military power.

belgium.s: Belgium is a country in northwestern Europe that became independent in 1830 and acquired a large colonial empire in Central Africa. King Leopold II's Congo Free State absorbed the territories of the Luba and Lunda states from the 1890s, and the region passed to Belgian state…

belgrade.s: Belgrade is a city at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers, now the capital of Serbia. A key frontier fortress controlling the route into central Europe, it was conquered by the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent in 1521.

bengal.s: Bengal is a region in the northeast of the Indian subcontinent, centred on the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers, and long one of its richest agricultural and commercial areas. It broke away from the Delhi Sultanate in 1339 and was never recovered by later sultans.

benin-bronze-plaques.s: The Benin bronze plaques are cast brass and bronze panels that once decorated the pillars of the royal palace in Benin City. They depict the oba, chiefs, warriors, ceremonies and Portuguese visitors.

benin-bronzes.s: The Benin Bronzes are thousands of cast metal plaques, heads and sculptures, together with ivory and other objects, made by guilds working for the royal court of the Benin Empire. The site dates the tradition to 1485–1897, from early contact with the Portuguese to the British…

benin-city.s: Benin City, historically known as Ubini, is a city in present-day southern Nigeria and was the capital of the Benin Empire. It was the seat of the oba, his palace and the craft guilds that produced the Benin Bronzes, and was protected by extensive earthen walls and moats.

benin-empire.s: The Benin Empire, also called the Kingdom of Benin, was a state in the forest region of present-day southern Nigeria ruled by the oba from Benin City. It reached its height between the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries, trading with the Portuguese and other Europeans and…

benin-expedition-of-1897.s: The Benin Expedition of 1897 was a British punitive military campaign against the Benin Empire, launched after the killing of a British party attempting to reach Benin City. British forces captured and burned the city, exiled Oba Ovonramwen and annexed the kingdom.

benito-mussolini.s: Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician who founded Fascism and ruled Italy as dictator from 1922 until 1943. He sought to build a new Roman empire, launching the invasion of Ethiopia in 1935 and proclaiming the Italian Empire in 1936.

benjamin-constant.s: Benjamin Constant was a Swiss-born French political thinker of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries and a leading liberal theorist. His idea of a neutral "moderating power" held by the monarch above the other branches of government influenced the constitution of…

benzoin-resin.s: Benzoin resin is an aromatic balsamic resin obtained from trees of the genus Styrax, used as incense, in perfume and in medicine. It was one of the forest products of the Sumatran interior, along with camphor and aromatic woods.

berber-revolt.s: The Berber Revolt was a series of uprisings in North Africa between 739 and 743 CE against the rule of the Umayyad Caliphate. It was triggered by grievances among Berber converts, including Arab officials' refusal to treat them as equals in the division of conquered land.

berbers.s: The Berbers, or Amazigh, are the indigenous peoples of North Africa, living across the Maghreb and the Sahara. Berber groups formed the core of several empires, including the Almoravid Empire, founded by Saharan Sanhaja tribes, and the Almohad Caliphate, rooted among the…

bernal-diaz-del-castillo.s: Bernal Díaz del Castillo was a Spanish conquistador who took part in Hernán Cortés's conquest of Mexico in the early sixteenth century. In old age he wrote a detailed eyewitness history of the conquest.

bernardino-de-sahagun.s: Bernardino de Sahagún was a Spanish Franciscan friar who worked in New Spain in the sixteenth century. With indigenous informants and assistants he compiled the General History of the Things of New Spain, known as the Florentine Codex, written in Nahuatl and Spanish.

bessus.s: Bessus was the Persian satrap of Bactria in the late Achaemenid period. After Alexander the Great's victory at Gaugamela, he murdered Darius III in 330 BCE and claimed the Persian throne.

beylerbey.s: A beylerbey, meaning "bey of beys", was the governor of a major province in the Ottoman Empire. Beylerbeys commanded the provincial cavalry and oversaw the sanjak governors beneath them.

beylik.s: A beylik was a Turkic principality ruled by a bey, especially one of the small states that emerged in Anatolia after the collapse of Seljuk authority in the thirteenth century. One of these, the beylik of Osman I in the Bithynian borderlands near Bursa, lay on the frontier…

bhonsles.s: The Bhonsles were a Maratha clan to which Shivaji, founder of the Maratha state, belonged. A branch of the family ruled Nagpur in central India as one of the great semi-independent Maratha houses, alongside the Gaekwads, Holkars and Scindias.

bhukti.s: A bhukti was a province in the administrative system of the Gupta Empire. Each bhukti was governed by an uparika, frequently a member of the royal family, and was divided into districts called vishayas.

bi-sheng.s: Bi Sheng was a Chinese artisan of the Song Dynasty credited with inventing movable type printing using ceramic characters around 1040 CE. His method is recorded in the writings of the scholar Shen Kuo.

bicameral-legislature.s: A bicameral legislature is a lawmaking body divided into two separate chambers or houses. The Meiji Constitution of 1889 created such a legislature, the Imperial Diet, in the Empire of Japan, with an elected lower house and an appointed upper house.

bida.s: Bida is a city in present-day central Nigeria, the capital of the Nupe emirate, which formed part of the Sokoto Caliphate in the nineteenth century. It was captured by British forces under Frederick Lugard in 1901.

bight-of-benin.s: The Bight of Benin is a bay of the Gulf of Guinea on the coast of West Africa, stretching roughly from present-day Ghana to the Niger Delta. In the era of the Atlantic slave trade it was known as the Slave Coast.

bilge-qaghan.s: Bilge Qaghan was a ruler of the Second Göktürk Khaganate who consolidated the state in the early eighth century. Under him a single exchange with the Tang emperor Xuanzong produced 100,000 bolts of silk for thirty horses, illustrating Göktürk extraction from China.

bindusara.s: Bindusara was the second emperor of the Maurya Empire, son of Chandragupta Maurya and father of Ashoka. He ruled in the early third century BCE.

bishapur.s: Bishapur was a city in southwestern Iran founded by the Sasanian king Shapur I in the third century CE. Its construction drew on the labour and engineering skills of Roman prisoners captured in Shapur's campaigns.

bishop.s: A bishop is a senior member of the Christian clergy who oversees a diocese and its priests. In the Aksumite Empire, Frumentius became the first bishop of Aksum after the adoption of Christianity.

bithynia.s: Bithynia is a historical region in northwestern Anatolia, bordering the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. In the late thirteenth century its Byzantine borderlands near Bursa were the home of the beylik of Osman I.

black-death.s: The Black Death was the pandemic of plague that swept across Eurasia and North Africa in the mid-fourteenth century, killing a large share of the population. It spread along the trade routes linked by the Pax Mongolica.

black-sea.s: The Black Sea is an inland sea between southeastern Europe and Anatolia, connected to the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles. It was a vital trade and strategic zone for the Byzantine Empire and the Khazar Khaganate, and the Ottoman Empire long controlled its…

black-ships.s: The Black Ships was the Japanese name for the Western vessels, especially the steam-powered warships of Commodore Matthew Perry's American squadron that entered Edo Bay in 1853. Perry demanded the opening of Japan to American commerce.

blekinge.s: Blekinge is a province in southeastern Sweden on the Baltic coast. Formerly Danish, it was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658, along with Scania, Halland and other territories.

board-of-agriculture.s: The Board of Agriculture was a government office of the Yuan Dynasty responsible for promoting farming. It produced agricultural handbooks and supported land reclamation and irrigation.

bodhisattva.s: A bodhisattva, in Buddhism, is a being who has attained great spiritual merit and seeks enlightenment for the benefit of all, a central ideal of Mahayana Buddhism. In Gandharan art, which grew from the Greek culture left by the Seleucid Empire, Greek sculptural style was…

boers.s: The Boers were the descendants of Dutch-speaking settlers in southern Africa, who founded independent republics in the Transvaal and Orange Free State in the nineteenth century. In the Second Boer War of 1899–1902, the British Empire needed around 450,000 troops to defeat…

bohdan-khmelnytsky.s: Bohdan Khmelnytsky was a Cossack leader who led a major uprising in Ukraine against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1648. The revolt caused catastrophic losses and led to an alliance with Muscovy.

bohemia.s: Bohemia is a historical region in central Europe forming the western part of the present-day Czech Republic, with Prague as its centre. It was a kingdom within the Holy Roman Empire, whose king was one of the imperial electors.

bohuslan.s: Bohuslän is a province on the west coast of present-day Sweden, formerly part of Norway under the Danish crown. It was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658.

bolivia.s: Bolivia is a country in central South America, which in the colonial period formed part of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru as the region of Upper Peru. It contained the silver mines of Potosí, worked by indigenous labour under the mita system.

bologna.s: Bologna is a city in northern Italy, home to one of the oldest universities in Europe. From the eleventh century its scholars studied the recovered Corpus Juris Civilis, the law code compiled under Justinian.

bombard.s: A bombard is a large early cannon, usually a muzzle-loader firing heavy stone balls, used mainly in sieges in the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. The Ottoman Empire employed huge bombards, notably at the siege of Constantinople in 1453.

bondu.s: Bondu is a region in eastern Senegal, near the upper Senegal and Falémé rivers. It lies close to the gold-bearing areas of West Africa.

book-of-exodus.s: The Book of Exodus is the second book of the Hebrew Bible, recounting the Israelites' departure from Egypt and the giving of the law at Sinai. Its legal section, known as the Book of the Covenant, shows parallels with the Code of Hammurabi.

book-of-the-covenant.s: The Book of the Covenant is the name scholars give to the collection of laws in the Book of Exodus (chapters 20 to 23) in the Hebrew Bible. Its provisions on injury, property and slavery closely parallel earlier Mesopotamian law codes, especially the Code of Hammurabi.

boran.s: Boran was a queen of the Sasanian Empire who briefly ruled in the early 630s CE, a daughter of Khosrow II. She was one of about a dozen claimants to the throne in the years after Khosrow's deposition in 628, including another queen, Azarmidokht.

borgu.s: Borgu is a region of West Africa straddling the border of present-day Benin and Nigeria, home to the Bariba people. Around 1535, after a defeat by the Nupe, the ruling dynasty of Oyo spent roughly eighty years in exile in Borgu.

borneo.s: Borneo is a large island in the Malay Archipelago of Southeast Asia, today divided between Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Its coastal ports were linked to the maritime trade networks of the archipelago.

bornholm.s: Bornholm is a Danish island in the Baltic Sea. It was ceded to Sweden by the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658, together with Scania, Blekinge, Halland and Norwegian provinces, at the height of the Swedish Empire.

bornu.s: Bornu was a state and region west of Lake Chad, the seat of the Kanem-Bornu Empire after its ruling dynasty moved there from Kanem in the late fourteenth century. Under rulers such as Idris Alooma it became a major Sahelian Islamic power.

borobudur.s: Borobudur is a monumental Mahayana Buddhist temple in central Java, built in the eighth and ninth centuries under the Sailendra dynasty. It is one of the largest Buddhist monuments in the world, decorated with extensive relief carvings.

boshin-war.s: The Boshin War was a Japanese civil war fought in 1868–1869 between forces loyal to the Tokugawa shogunate and a coalition led by the Satsuma and Choshu domains acting in the name of the emperor. The imperial forces defeated the shogunal army and its French-trained troops.

bosnia-herzegovina.s: Bosnia-Herzegovina is a region in the western Balkans, ruled by the Ottoman Empire for centuries. It was occupied by Austria-Hungary in 1878 and formally annexed in 1908, a move that heightened Balkan tensions.

bosphorus.s: The Bosphorus is a narrow strait in northwestern Turkey connecting the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and separating Europe from Asia. Constantinople stood on its European shore, controlling traffic between the two seas.

boston.s: Boston is a city in the northeastern United States, capital of Massachusetts. Its museums hold Persian carpets from the classical period of Safavid weaving.

bourba.s: Bourba was the title of the supreme ruler, or emperor, of the Jolof Empire in Senegambia. The bourba exercised nominal supremacy over a network of semi-autonomous rulers of the constituent kingdoms.

bourbon-reforms.s: The Bourbon Reforms were a programme of administrative, fiscal and military changes introduced in Spain and its American colonies by the Bourbon kings in the eighteenth century. They sought to rationalise colonial government, tighten royal control and increase revenue.

brahmins.s: Brahmins are the priestly and learned class at the top of the traditional Hindu social hierarchy, responsible for religious ritual and the transmission of sacred knowledge. Under the Gupta Empire they received land grants and royal patronage.

brandenburg.s: Brandenburg is a historical region of northeastern Germany around Berlin. Its ruler, the Margrave of Brandenburg, was one of the seven electors who chose the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire.

brazilian-empire.s: The Brazilian Empire was a constitutional monarchy in South America from 1822 to 1889, founded when Pedro, son of the Portuguese king, declared Brazil's independence and became Emperor Pedro I. Under Pedro II it achieved relative stability through a constitution that gave the…

brazilian-gold-rush.s: The Brazilian Gold Rush was the large-scale exploitation of gold deposits in Minas Gerais, Brazil, following discoveries in the 1690s, with diamond finds following after 1729. It produced a spectacular revenue surge for the Portuguese crown and funded João V's lavish court.

brazilwood.s: Brazilwood is a tropical tree whose dense red heartwood was valued in early modern Europe as the source of a red dye for textiles. It was the first major export of Portuguese Brazil, and the colony was named after it.

brazzaville.s: Brazzaville is a city on the Congo River, now the capital of the Republic of the Congo. It was founded in the 1880s and became the headquarters of French Equatorial Africa.

breech-loading-rifle.s: A breech-loading rifle is a firearm loaded at the rear of the barrel rather than through the muzzle, allowing much faster reloading, especially when lying down. Such weapons spread widely among European armies in the later nineteenth century.

bremen.s: Bremen is a port city on the Weser River in northwestern Germany and was a leading member of the Hanseatic League. As a free imperial city it was one of the commercial centres of the Holy Roman Empire.

brigade.s: A brigade is a military formation made up of several battalions or regiments, smaller than a division. Gustavus Adolphus of the Swedish Empire reorganised the massive tercio squares into smaller, more manoeuvrable brigades of musketeers and pikemen.

brihaspati-smriti.s: The Brihaspati Smriti is a Sanskrit legal text of the Dharmashastra tradition, attributed to the sage Brihaspati. Compiled or refined during the Gupta period, it dealt with civil and criminal law, property, inheritance and judicial procedure.

britain.s: Britain, or Great Britain, is an island off northwestern Europe comprising England, Scotland and Wales, united as a single kingdom from 1707. It was a province of the Roman Empire and later the metropolitan centre of the British Empire, the largest empire in history.

british-conquest-of-kano.s: The British conquest of Kano took place in February 1903, when forces of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria under Frederick Lugard captured the city after a brief engagement. The defenders had no answer to British Maxim guns.

british-empire.s: The British Empire comprised the dominions, colonies, protectorates and other territories ruled or administered by Britain from the late sixteenth to the twentieth century. At its height it was the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land.

british-india.s: British India refers to the territories of the Indian subcontinent ruled directly by Britain, first through the East India Company and from 1858 by the crown. It expanded by conquest and annexation, absorbing the Sikh Empire after the Anglo-Sikh wars of the 1840s.

british-museum.s: The British Museum is a public museum in London founded in 1753, holding one of the world's largest collections of human history and culture. It houses Assyrian palace reliefs, including the lion hunt reliefs of Ashurbanipal from Nineveh.

british-raj.s: The British Raj was the system of direct British crown rule over the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947, after the East India Company's rule ended following the rebellion of 1857. It was headed by a viceroy and administered by the Indian Civil Service.

british-south-africa-company.s: The British South Africa Company was a chartered company founded by Cecil Rhodes in 1889 to acquire and exploit territory in south-central Africa. It occupied the Zimbabwe plateau in 1890, creating the colony later named Rhodesia.

bronze.s: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and the term is also used loosely for related copper alloys such as brass. In the Bronze Age it was the principal metal for weapons, tools and prestige goods in empires such as the Egyptian New Kingdom, the Hittite Empire and Mitanni.

bronze-age.s: The Bronze Age is the period in which bronze was the dominant material for tools and weapons, in the Near East and eastern Mediterranean lasting from about the late fourth millennium to around 1200 BCE. Its late phase saw a system of great powers including the Egyptian Empire…

bronze-casting.s: Bronze casting is the technique of shaping objects by pouring molten copper alloy into moulds, often using the lost-wax method. In the Benin Empire, casting was controlled by a royal guild working for the oba.

bronze-working.s: Bronze-working is the craft of producing tools, weapons and ornaments from bronze, an alloy of copper and tin. Elam, with access to metal resources of the Iranian plateau, developed an important metalworking tradition.

brusilov-offensive.s: The Brusilov Offensive was a major Russian attack on the Eastern Front from June to September 1916 during the First World War, led by General Alexei Brusilov along a front of about 480 kilometres. It inflicted enormous losses on the Austro-Hungarian army, estimated at 600,000…

budapest.s: Budapest is the capital of Hungary on the Danube, formed in 1873 by the union of Buda, Óbuda and Pest. It was the Hungarian capital within the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.

buddhism.s: Buddhism is a religion and philosophy based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, which originated in northern India around the fifth century BCE. Promoted by Ashoka of the Maurya Empire, it spread across Asia and became a pillar of states such as the Srivijaya…

buke-shohatto.s: The Buke shohatto, or Laws for Military Houses, were regulations issued by the Tokugawa shogunate, first in 1615 and revised several times later, to govern the conduct of the daimyo and samurai. They controlled castle building, marriages between domains and other activities.

bukhara.s: Bukhara is a city in present-day Uzbekistan, one of the great oasis centres of the Silk Road and of Islamic learning in Central Asia. It was sacked by the Mongols during the destruction of the Khwarazmian Empire and later fell under the Chagatai and Timurid empires.

bulala.s: The Bulala were a people of the Lake Fitri region east of Lake Chad. In the late fourteenth century their pressure forced the Sayfawa dynasty of Kanem to move westward to Bornu, where the state was reconstituted as Kanem-Bornu.

bulgaria.s: Bulgaria is a country in southeastern Europe whose medieval Bulgarian states were major rivals of Byzantium. Basil II reconquered Bulgaria in the early eleventh century, restoring the Byzantine Empire's control of the Balkans, and Bulgaria later adopted Byzantine Orthodox…

bulgars.s: The Bulgars were a Turkic-speaking nomadic people of the Pontic-Caspian steppe who emerged in the early medieval period. Some founded the First Bulgarian state on the Danube in the seventh century, while others settled on the middle Volga.

bumin-qaghan.s: Bumin Qaghan was the founder of the Göktürk Empire and a leader of the Ashina clan, originally a vassal of the Rouran Khaganate. After crushing a Uyghur revolt in 546 CE, he was refused a Rouran princess in marriage and rebelled.

bundelkhand.s: Bundelkhand is a hilly region of central India, between the Ganges plain and the Vindhya range. In the eighteenth century, Maratha armies under Peshwa Baji Rao I extended their power into Bundelkhand, along with Malwa and Gujarat.

bundesrat.s: The Bundesrat was the federal council of the German Empire, made up of delegates of the governments of the member states. It shared legislative authority with the elected Reichstag.

burakumin.s: The burakumin are a Japanese outcaste group, descended from communities that performed occupations considered ritually impure, such as butchery, leatherwork and the handling of the dead. Under the Tokugawa Shogunate they were placed at the bottom of a rigid legal status…

bure.s: Bure, or Buré, is a gold-bearing region on the upper Niger near the present-day border of Guinea and Mali. With Bambuk, it was one of the main sources of West African gold carried across the Sahara to Mediterranean markets.

bureau-of-military-affairs.s: The Bureau of Military Affairs was one of the three central organs of government of the Song Dynasty, alongside the Secretariat-Chancellery and the Finance Commission. It was headed by civilian officials and oversaw military administration.

bureaucratic-administration.s: Bureaucratic administration refers to government through trained, salaried officials organised in offices with defined functions, records and procedures, rather than through personal or tribal loyalties alone. It was a recurring basis of imperial strength, allowing states to…

burghers.s: Burghers were the citizens of chartered towns in medieval and early modern Europe, typically merchants and master craftsmen with civic rights. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth the dominant nobility restricted burgher political rights and economic protections.

burgundy.s: Burgundy is a historical region of eastern France and the name of a powerful late medieval duchy whose lands also included the Low Countries. Through the marriage of Mary of Burgundy to Maximilian of Habsburg, the Burgundian inheritance passed to the Habsburgs.

burma.s: Burma, now Myanmar, is a country in mainland Southeast Asia. The Qing Empire fought a series of costly and unsuccessful wars against Burma in the 1760s.

burmi.s: Burmi is a site in northeastern Nigeria where the last independent Sultan of Sokoto, Muhammadu Attahiru I, was killed in battle with British forces in July 1903. He had refused submission and retreated eastward in a hijra recalling dan Fodio's foundational migration.

bursa.s: Bursa is a city in northwestern Anatolia, near the Sea of Marmara. Osman I's beylik emerged in the Bithynian borderlands near the city, and it was captured by the Ottomans in 1326.

bushehr.s: Bushehr is a port city on the Persian Gulf coast of southern Iran. In the eighteenth century, together with Bandar Abbas, it handled Persian Gulf trade under the Afsharid Empire.

bushido.s: Bushido, meaning "the way of the warrior", is the code of conduct and ethics associated with the Japanese samurai, stressing loyalty, honour, discipline and martial skill. It was codified largely during the peaceful Edo period.

bushime-river.s: The Bushime River is a river in the southeast of present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo. Luba tradition records that the founder Kalala Ilunga expanded his realm westward as far as the Bushime River.

bushire.s: Bushire is an older European spelling of Bushehr, a port on the Persian Gulf coast of southern Iran. Under the Zand Empire, the British East India Company and the Dutch VOC maintained commercial presences there.

buyid-dynasty.s: The Buyid dynasty was a Shia Iranian dynasty from Daylam that controlled much of Iran and Iraq in the tenth and eleventh centuries. After taking Baghdad in 945, the Buyids ruled while keeping the Abbasid caliphs as figureheads.

byrsa.s: Byrsa is the hill at the centre of ancient Carthage, in present-day Tunisia, on which the city's citadel stood. According to legend, Queen Dido was granted as much land as an ox-hide could cover and cut the hide into thin strips to encircle the hill, the name being linked to…

byzantine-commonwealth.s: The Byzantine commonwealth is a term used by historians for the community of Orthodox Christian peoples and states culturally shaped by Byzantium, including Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania and Georgia. These societies adopted Byzantine religion, liturgy, law and artistic forms.

byzantine-empire.s: The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the Roman Empire in the eastern Mediterranean, ruled from Constantinople from the fourth century until the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Greek in language and Orthodox Christian in religion, it preserved Roman law and classical…

byzantine-iconoclasm.s: Byzantine Iconoclasm refers to two periods, 730–787 CE and 815–843 CE, during which Byzantine emperors banned the veneration of religious images and destroyed many icons. The policy provoked bitter religious and political conflict within the Byzantine Empire and strained…

byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628.s: The Byzantine-Sasanian War of 602–628 CE was the last and most destructive war between the Byzantine Empire and the Sasanian Empire. Sasanian armies under Khosrow II conquered Syria, Palestine and Egypt, before Heraclius counter-attacked and won at Nineveh in 627.

byzantion.s: Byzantion was an ancient Greek city on the European shore of the Bosphorus, founded by colonists from Megara. The emperor Constantine I refounded it as Constantinople in the fourth century CE, making it the new capital of the Roman world.
